content: The implementation and monitoring of the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations for tuberculosis (TB) treatment are being systematically integrated into global TB data collection efforts. These recommendations are reviewed annually as part of the WHO Global TB Data Monitoring initiative. The WHO plans to update its guidelines every five years or sooner if new evidence necessitates revisions. The WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis include contributions from a diverse group of global experts. These experts represent various fields, including clinical practice, pharmacology, epidemiology, laboratory science, and public health. They are involved in the development and periodic updates of treatment guidelines for drug-resistant TB, rifampicin-resistant TB, multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), and isoniazid-resistant TB. The guidelines also address the treatment of drug-susceptible TB and patient care. The guideline development process involves a Guideline Development Group (GDG) comprising clinicians, researchers, program managers, and technical experts from institutions worldwide. For example, Holger Schünemann, a GRADE methodologist from McMaster University in Canada, chaired the GDG for the 2020 update of the drug-resistant TB treatment guidelines. Other notable contributors include Rafael Laniado-Laborin, a clinician from Mexico's National TB Program, and Susan Abdel Rahman, a pediatric pharmacologist from the United States. The guidelines also incorporate input from laboratory specialists, such as Daniela Cirillo from the San Raffaele Supranational TB Reference Laboratory in Italy, and clinical trial experts like Charles Daley from National Jewish Health in the United States. Additionally, experts in pharmacology, such as Kelly Dooley from Johns Hopkins University, and public health specialists, including Agnes Gebhard from the KNCV Tuberculosis Foundation in the Netherlands, contribute to the evidence-based recommendations. The WHO guidelines are supported by evidence reviewers and observers who provide critical analysis and feedback. These include epidemiologists, health economists, and behavioral scientists from institutions such as McGill University in Canada and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine in the United Kingdom. Observers from organizations like the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria also participate in the process. The guidelines are further informed by regional and national TB program representatives, ensuring that the recommendations are practical and applicable across diverse healthcare settings. For instance, representatives from countries such as South Africa, India, China, and Brazil contribute their expertise in managing TB at the programmatic level. In summary, the WHO's TB treatment guidelines are the result of a collaborative effort involving a multidisciplinary team of global experts. These guidelines are regularly updated to reflect the latest scientific evidence and to address the evolving challenges of TB management worldwide.
